L25: # 【7†Accounts】
L26: 
L27: Copy Markdown Open
L28: 
L29: An account is Solana's fundamental data unit for storing state. The network stores all state in a key-value store where each key is a 32-byte address and each value is an account.
L30: 
L31: 【19†Image: Diagram of 3 accounts and their addresses. Includes the account structure definition.】Diagram of 3 accounts and their addresses. Includes the account structure definition.
L32: 【8†Account Structure Account addresses (public key, PDA), the five fields every account contains, storage balance, and the deprecated rent field, with an interactive code walkthrough.】【9†Account Types Program accounts (executable code), data accounts (program state), system accounts, and sysvars (cluster-wide state).】【10†Modification Rules Runtime-enforced rules for lamports, data, owner, executable flag, and borrows.】【11†Account Runtime Account loading validation, BPF serialization format, and deserialization.】
L33: ## 【20†Key facts】
L34:   * Structure: Every account has the same 【8†five fields】: lamports, data, owner, executable, rent_epoch.
L35:   * Address: Each account is identified by a unique 32-byte address (either an Ed25519 public key or a 【16†PDA】).
L36:   * Ownership: Only the account's owner program can modify its data or debit lamports. Any program can credit lamports to any writable account.
L37:   * Account storage: Every account must hold a refundable minimum lamport balance proportional to its data size to remain onchain.
L38: ## 【21†Limits】
L39: Limit  | Value  | Source
L40: --- | --- | ---
L41: Max account data size  | 10 MiB (10,485,760 bytes)  | 【22†`MAX_ACCOUNT_DATA_LEN`†github.com】
L42: Max data growth per instruction  | 10 KiB (10,240 bytes)  | 【23†`MAX_PERMITTED_DATA_INCREASE`†github.com】
L43: Max data growth per transaction  | 20 MiB (20,971,520 bytes)  | 【24†`MAX_ACCOUNT_DATA_GROWTH_PER_TRANSACTION`†github.com】
L44: Account base storage overhead  | 64 bytes per account  | 【25†`TRANSACTION_ACCOUNT_BASE_SIZE`†github.com】
L45: Address size  | 32 bytes (Ed25519 public key)  | --
L46: Minimum storage balance (formula)  | (account_size + 128) * 3,480 lamports/byte-year * 2 years  | 【26†`minimum_balance()`†github.com】

L25: # 【12†Fee Structure】
L26: 
L27: Copy Markdown Open
L28: 
L29: Summary
L30: 
L31: Total fee = base fee (5,000 lamports/signature, 50% burned) + priority fee (CU_price * CU_limit / 1M lamports, 100% to validator). Charged whether the transaction succeeds or fails.
L32: ## 【17†Fee calculation algorithm】
L33: 
L34: The total fee for a transaction is computed by 【18†`calculate_fee_details`†github.com】:
L35: 
L36: Total fee formula
L37: 
L38:     total_fee = base_fee + prioritization_fee
L39: 
L40: The inputs are the transaction message, the current `lamports_per_signature` (currently 5,000), and the prioritization fee derived from compute budget instructions. The total fee is deducted from the fee payer before execution begins. If the transaction fails, the fee is still charged.
L41: ## 【19†Base fee】
L42: 
L43: The base fee covers the cost of Ed25519 signature verification plus any precompile signature verifications. Every signature in the transaction is charged, including signatures verified by the Ed25519, Secp256k1, and Secp256r1 precompile programs.
L44: 
L45: The 【20†`calculate_signature_fee`†github.com】 function computes:
L46: Base fee formula
L47: 
L48:     signature_count = num_transaction_signatures
L49: 
L50: 
L51:                     + num_ed25519_signatures
L52: 
L53: 
L54:                     + num_secp256k1_signatures
L55: 
L56: 
L57:                     + num_secp256r1_signatures   (if feature enabled)
L58: 
L59: 
L60: 
L61: 
L62: 
L63:     base_fee = signature_count * lamports_per_signature
L64:   * `num_transaction_signatures`: the number of Ed25519 signatures on the transaction (typically one per signer).
L65:   * `num_ed25519_signatures`, `num_secp256k1_signatures`, `num_secp256r1_signatures`: signatures verified by the corresponding precompile programs.
L66:   * `lamports_per_signature`: currently 【21†5,000 lamports†github.com】.
L67: ### 【22†Fee distribution】
L68: 
L69: The base fee and prioritization fee are distributed differently. The 【23†`calculate_reward_and_burn_fee_details`†github.com】 function in the runtime computes:
L70: 
L71: Fee distribution
L72: 
L73:     burn_amount     = transaction_fee * 50 / 100
L74: 
L75: 
L76:     validator_share = (transaction_fee - burn_amount) + priority_fee
L77:   * Base fee (transaction_fee): 50% is 【24†burned†github.com】 (removed from circulating supply) and 50% goes to the block-producing validator. The burn percent is 【25†`DEFAULT_BURN_PERCENT = 50`†github.com】.
L78:   * Prioritization fee: 100% goes to the validator (none is burned), per 【26†SIMD-0096†github.com】.
L79: 
L80: The validator's total reward for a transaction is:
L81: 
L82:     validator_reward = (base_fee / 2) + prioritization_fee
L83: ## 【27†Prioritization fee】
L84: 
L85: The prioritization fee is an optional fee that increases the scheduling priority of a transaction. A compute unit (CU) is a unit of computation that the runtime meters during transaction execution. Every operation (arithmetic, memory access, syscall) costs a fixed number of CUs. You can set the prioritization fee by including compute budget instructions in your transaction. (See the 【11†How to Use Priority Fees guide】 for details.)
L86: ### 【28†Prioritization fee formula】
L87: 
L88: The 【29†`get_prioritization_fee`†github.com】 function computes:
L89: 
L90: Prioritization fee formula
L91: 
L92:     micro_lamport_fee = compute_unit_price * compute_unit_limit
L93: 
L94: 
L95:     prioritization_fee = ceil(micro_lamport_fee / 1,000,000)
L96: Variable  | Description  | Default
L97: --- | --- | ---
L98: `compute_unit_price`  | Micro-lamports per CU, set via `SetComputeUnitPrice`  | 0 micro-lamports
L99: `compute_unit_limit`  | Maximum CUs the transaction may consume, set via `SetComputeUnitLimit`  | Sum of per-instruction defaults
L100: `1,000,000`  | Conversion factor from micro-lamports to lamports (【30†`MICRO_LAMPORTS_PER_LAMPORT`†github.com】)  | --
L101: 
L102: v1 transactions set the fee directly
L103: This price-times-limit formula applies to legacy and v0 transactions. In the 【31†v1 format】, the priority fee is an absolute total in lamports set directly in the message config — no per-CU price, no multiplication, no rounding.
L104: ### 【32†Compute unit limit】
L105: 
L106: The compute unit limit is the maximum number of CUs a transaction may consume. If no 【33†`SetComputeUnitLimit`†github.com】 instruction is included, the default is calculated from the number and type of instructions (200,000 CUs per non-builtin instruction, 3,000 per builtin). See 【13†Compute Budget】 for details on the default calculation.
L107: The priority fee is based on the requested CU limit, not actual CU usage. Setting a higher limit than needed means paying for unused compute units.
L108: ### 【34†Compute unit price】
L109: 
L110: The compute unit price is an optional amount of micro-lamports paid for each requested CU. The CU price directly determines the prioritization fee. To set the CU price, include a 【35†`SetComputeUnitPrice`†github.com】 instruction in your transaction.
L111: 
L112: The default CU price is 0, meaning the default prioritization fee is also 0.
L113: 
L114: For real-time CU price estimates, see the priority fee API providers below.
L115: Provider  | Priority Fee API
L116: --- | ---
L117: 【36†Helius†www.helius.dev】  | 【37†Documentation†docs.helius.dev】
L118: 【38†QuickNode†www.quicknode.com】  | 【39†Documentation†marketplace.quicknode.com】
L119: 【40†Triton†triton.one】  | 【41†Documentation†docs.triton.one】
L120: ### 【42†Transaction scheduling priority】
L121: 
L122: The scheduler ranks transactions using the 【43†`calculate_priority_and_cost`†github.com】 function:
L123: 
L124: Transaction priority formula
L125: 
L126:     Priority = reward * 1,000,000 / (cost + 1)
L127:   * reward: the validator's fee income = prioritization fee + non-burned portion of the base fee. Computed by 【44†`calculate_reward_for_transaction`†github.com】.
L128:   * cost: the scheduler's 【45†estimated CU cost†github.com】 (signature costs + write lock costs + instruction data costs + program execution costs + loaded accounts data size cost). See 【46†Compute Budget】 for details.
L129:   * 1,000,000: a multiplier to preserve precision, since cost often exceeds reward in raw lamports.
L130:   * +1: prevents division by zero.
L131: The priority determines the order in which transactions are dequeued from the scheduler's buffer for execution.
L132: ## 【47†Example: Setting the CU limit and CU price】

L21: 
L22: Effective May 1, 2026: Trading data is only available to users who subscribe with a 【2†PumpPortal API key】.

L24: There is no charge for data received from the subscribeNewToken and subscribeMigration methods.
L25: 
L26: Data received from methods subscribeTokenTrade or subscribeAccountTrade is metered at the following rate: every 10000 trades streamed will incur a 0.01 SOL charge to the wallet linked to their API key.
L27: ### Local Transaction API【12†​】
L28: 
L29: We take a 0.5% fee on each Local trade. (Note: the fee is calculated before any slippage, so the actual fee amount may not be exactly 0.5% of the final trade value.)
L30: ### Lightning Transaction API【13†​】
L31: 
L32: We take a 1% fee on each Lightning trade. (Note: the fee is calculated before any slippage, so the actual fee amount may not be exactly 1% of the final trade value.)
L33: 
L34: The above fees do not include Solana network fees, or any fees charged by the Pump.fun bonding curve.

L21: Crypto Spot Trading Fees
L22: # Crypto Spot Trading Fees
L23: While Alpaca stock trading remains commission-free, crypto trading includes a small fee per trade dependent on your executed volume and order type. Any market or exchange consists of two parties, buyers and sellers. When you place an order to buy crypto on the Alpaca Exchange, there is someone else on the other side of the trade selling what you want to buy. The seller's posted order on the order book is providing liquidity to the exchange and allows for the trade to take place.
L24: Note, that both buyers and sellers can be makers or takers depending on the order entered and current quote of the coin. A maker is someone who adds liquidity, and the order gets placed on the order book. A Taker on the other hand removes the liquidity by placing a market or marketable limit order which executes against posted orders.
L25: See the below table with volume-tiered fee pricing:
L26: 
L27: Tier  | 30D Crypto Volume (USD)  | Maker  | Take
L28: --- | --- | --- | ---
L29: 1  | 0 - 100,000  | 0.15%  | 0.25%
L30: 2  | 100,000 - 500,000  | 0.12%  | 0.22%
L31: 3  | 500,000 - 1,000,000  | 0.10%  | 0.20%
L32: 4  | 1,000,000 - 10,000,000  | 0.08%  | 0.18%
L33: 5  | 10,000,000- 25,000,000  | 0.05%  | 0.15%
L34: 6  | 25,000,000 - 50,000,000  | 0.02%  | 0.13%
L35: 7  | 50,000,000 - 100,000,000  | 0.02%  | 0.12%
L36: 8  | 100,000,000+  | 0.00%  | 0.10%
L37: The crypto fee will be charged on the credited crypto asset/fiat (what you receive) per trade. Some examples:
L38: 
L39:   * Buy `ETH/BTC`, you receive `ETH`, the fee is denominated in `ETH`
L40:   * Sell `ETH/BTC`, you receive `BTC`, the fee is denominated in `BTC`
L41:   * Buy `ETH/USD`, you receive `ETH`, the fee is denominated in `ETH`
L42:   * Sell `ETH/USD`, you receive `USD`, the fee is denominated in `USD`
L43: 
L44: To get the fees incurred from crypto trading you can use Activities API to query `activity_type` by `CFEE` or `FEE`.
L45: See below example of CFEE object:
L46: 
L47: [Button: JSON]
L48: 
L49:     `{
L50:         "id": "20220812000000000::53be51ba-46f9-43de-b81f-576f241dc680",
L51:         "activity_type": "CFEE",
L52:         "date": "2022-08-12",
L53:         "net_amount": "0",
L54:         "description": "Coin Pair Transaction Fee (Non USD)",
L55:         "symbol": "ETHUSD",
L56:         "qty": "-0.000195",
L57:         "price": "1884.5",
L58:         "status": "executed"
L59:     }`
L60: Fees are currently calculated and posted end of day. If you query on same day of trade you might not get results. We will be providing an update for fee posting to be real-time in the near future.
